sm: Host Kyle Peterson, with columnists Kim Strassel and Alicia Finley, discusses House Republican leadership after the midterm losses. Speaker Mike Johnson says he will not run for minority leader, citing prayer and reflection and noting that Nancy Pelosi was the only modern speaker to stay on in the minority. Strassel praises him for stepping aside and for holding a difficult conference together. She describes the race between Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan. Scalise argues he is tested and has experience in the minority, but many of his allies were moderates who just lost their seats. Jordan argues the party needs a fresh approach and a forward agenda, and he has the Freedom Caucus behind him but must reassure moderate skeptics.

Alicia Finley discusses the failure of California's ballot initiative for a one-time wealth tax, which trailed by about four percentage points even as Democrats won every statewide office and expanded their supermajorities. She says the backers, including the SEIU health care workers union, have not conceded and may try again in 2028, or push a big income tax increase through the legislature. At least seven billionaires holding about 580 billion dollars have already said they are leaving, and she warns that when AI-driven capital gains revenue fades, the state will face deficits and broader tax hikes. Asked whether California's initiative process is too easy to use, she says the larger problem is Democratic control of the state. She points to the 2024 effort to require two-thirds voter approval for tax increases, which Governor Gavin Newsom and allies got removed from the ballot.

Kim Strassel says the midterms undercut the claim that billionaires buy elections. Elon Musk reportedly spent about 220 million dollars in Texas, and Republicans lost there anyway. Republicans outspent Democrats by more than 135 million dollars in Texas, 82 million in Ohio, 37 million in Maine and 26 million in Michigan, yet still lost. She says money is only one factor, and that Republicans lacked a forward agenda. She blames Ken Paxton's scandals in Texas and Susan Collins's ties to Donald Trump in Maine. Kyle Peterson notes that record midterm spending of about 12 billion dollars is comparable to what Americans spend on vitamins or cookies. Alicia Finley then begins describing the Supreme Court case Department of Labor versus Sun Valley Orchards, in which a New Jersey farm was fined about 550,000 dollars over worker housing and meal arrangements.

Finley explains that the fine was upheld through the Labor Department's own administrative process, and the farm went out of business in 2021. The orchard now argues that the Seventh Amendment guarantees a jury trial, relying on the 2024 Jarkesy decision on the SEC. The government says Jarkesy does not apply because the case involves public rights tied to immigration and the guest worker program. The hosts play an exchange in which Justice Samuel Alito presses the orchard's lawyer on how far the immigration exception extends. Strassel says the claim is a breach of private contracts with workers, a traditional common law matter. She notes the Third Circuit said the case falls outside the heartland of non-Article Three adjudication. The hosts conclude that a ruling for the farm would strengthen Jarkesy and the separation of powers.
